\chapter{Before a Postposition, Everything Changes}
\label{ch:ur-before-a-postposition}
\hlchaptermodality{23}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put something in a room, on a thing, or to a person -- and I know why the noun changes shape before I do it.}

The book's whole vocabulary becomes placeable for the first time: a pantry, a wardrobe and five kinds of weather that could only ever be named can now be put somewhere, and the postpositions the reader has been reading since chapter three finally have their rule stated.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kamrā]{\ur{کمرہ} (kamrā) — room}

\label{lesson:UR-C23-kamra}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{this}. Then say \textbf{black}, and say what its last vowel is doing.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the two items before this one — \emph{kyā kahā?}, \emph{ārām se}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{کمرہ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{یہ} \ur{کمرہ}} — \emph{yih kamrā} — \textbf{this room.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{پرانا} \ur{کمرہ}} — \emph{purānā kamrā} — \textbf{an old room.}
\end{quote}

Twenty-two chapters, and this book has named a mother, a brother, a friend, four foods, four garments and five kinds of weather — and not one \textbf{place}. A learner could say who they were and could not say where anything was.

\textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} is said \emph{kamrā} and ends in the vowel \emph{-ā}, even though the last letter on the page is \textbf{\ur{ہ}}. That is worth pausing on: at the end of a word like this the gol he is not an \emph{h} at all — it is how Urdu writes a final \emph{-ā}. You met the same letter in this job inside \emph{shukriyā}.

So \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} is one of the masculine nouns whose adjectives agree with it: \textbf{\ur{کالا} \ur{کمرہ}}, \textbf{\ur{پرانا} \ur{کمرہ}}. The \textbf{-\ur{ا}} on the adjective is answering the \emph{-ā} on the noun, exactly as chapter thirteen showed.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} is \textbf{Portuguese}. \emph{Câmara} came ashore with the sixteenth-century sea trade, and it is the same Latin \emph{camera} — a vaulted room — that English borrowed twice: once as \textbf{chamber}, and once as \textbf{camera}, because a \emph{camera obscura} is a dark room.

So this word arrived by ship, where \textbf{\ur{نیلا}} arrived by land — the Sanskrit indigo that also gives English \emph{aniline}. Urdu takes words from every direction it has ever been reached from.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kamrā}
  \item \emph{yih kamrā}, then \emph{voh kamrā}
  \item with an adjective that agrees — \emph{kālā kamrā}, \emph{nīlā kamrā}, \emph{purānā kamrā}
  \item the English cousins — \emph{chamber}, \emph{camera}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which language did \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} come from, and by what route? (\textbf{Portuguese}, by sea.) Which two English words share its Latin root? (\textbf{Chamber} and \textbf{camera}.) And what does its final \textbf{-\ur{ا}} tell an adjective to do? (\textbf{End in -\ur{ا} too}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kamre]{\ur{کمرے} (kamre) — the shape a noun takes before a postposition}

\label{lesson:UR-C23-oblique}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{this room}. Then say \textbf{your name}, and notice the little word standing between \textbf{\ur{آپ}} and \textbf{\ur{نام}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the noun changes first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} — \emph{kamrā} — a room, standing on its own.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کمرے} \ur{کے} \ur{لیے}} — \emph{kamre ke liye} — \textbf{for the room.}
\end{quote}

Look at what happened to the noun. It was \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} and it is now \textbf{\ur{کمرے}}, and nothing about the meaning changed. The final \emph{-ā} became \textbf{-\ur{ے}} because a postposition was coming.

This is the single most important rule in Urdu grammar that a learner can be taught, and this book has used it since chapter three without stating it. \textbf{\ur{آپ} \ur{کا} \ur{نام}} and \textbf{\ur{کے} \ur{لیے}} are both postpositions, and both have been quietly demanding this change all along.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two shapes, and only two}]
Sanskrit inflected a noun eight ways. Urdu kept \textbf{one} distinction:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{shape} & \textbf{when} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
\textbf{direct} & the noun is a subject, or alone & \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} \\
\textbf{oblique} & a postposition follows it & \textbf{\ur{کمرے}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And the adjective goes with it. \textbf{\ur{کالا} \ur{کمرہ}} becomes \textbf{\ur{کالے} \ur{کمرے}}: the adjective is agreeing with the noun's new shape, not merely with its gender.

Nouns not ending in \emph{-ā} do not visibly change — \textbf{\ur{ماں}} is \textbf{\ur{ماں}} either way. A reader can go a long way without noticing the shape-change, and then be unable to build a phrase.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \emph{kamrā}, then \emph{kamre ke liye}
  \item with the adjective following it over — \emph{kālā kamrā}, then \emph{kāle kamre ke liye}
  \item \emph{purāne kamre ke liye}
  \item the one that does not move — \emph{māṅ}, and \emph{māṅ ke liye}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What makes a noun change shape? (\textbf{A postposition coming after it}.) What does \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} become? (\textbf{\ur{کمرے}}.) Does the adjective follow it over? (\textbf{Yes} — \textbf{\ur{کالے} \ur{کمرے}}.) And which nouns do not visibly change? (\textbf{Those not ending in \emph{-ā}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ko]{\ur{کو} (ko) — to, and the one it happens to}

\label{lesson:UR-C23-ko}



\begin{quote}
What happens to \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} when a postposition follows it? Then say the sentence from chapter eight that means \textbf{I like mangoes}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{کو}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ماں} \ur{کو}} — \emph{māṅ ko} — \textbf{to the mother}, or \textbf{the mother}, as the one it happens to.
\end{quote}

Chapter eight taught \emph{mujhe ām pasand haiṅ} — \emph{mangoes are pleasing to me} — and then left you unable to say it about anybody else, because \emph{mujhe} looked like one word.

It is not. \emph{Mujhe} is \emph{mujh} plus \textbf{\ur{کو}}, fused so long ago that the seam has closed. Now that you have the postposition on its own, the frame opens to everybody:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ماں} \ur{کو}} \emph{ām pasand haiṅ} — \emph{māṅ ko ām pasand haiṅ} — \textbf{mother likes mangoes.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Mujhe} and \emph{pasand} stay in romanization here. Between them they need three letters the script ladder has not reached — \emph{jīm}, \emph{do chashmī he} and \emph{dāl} — and this book does not print a letter before it has taught it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two jobs, one word}]
\textbf{\ur{کو}} marks the person a thing is \textbf{given to}, and the person a thing is \textbf{done to}. English needs \emph{to} for the first and word order alone for the second; Urdu uses one postposition for both.

And it takes the oblique in front of it, like every postposition:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} $\to$ \textbf{\ur{کمرے} \ur{کو}}
\end{itemize}

A postposition never touches a direct-shape noun. That rule has no exceptions and it is worth over-learning now, because six more postpositions are coming.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{māṅ ko}
  \item the frame, opened — \emph{māṅ ko ām pasand haiṅ}
  \item the fused one beside the free one — \emph{mujhe}, then \emph{māṅ ko}
  \item taking the oblique — \emph{kamre ko}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two pieces is \emph{mujhe} made of? (\emph{Mujh} and \textbf{\ur{کو}}.) What does \textbf{\ur{کو}} mark? (\textbf{The one a thing is given or done to}.) And what shape must the noun in front of it be in? (\textbf{Oblique}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[meṅ]{\ur{میں} (meṅ) — in}

\label{lesson:UR-C23-mein}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{to the mother}. Then say \textbf{I am well}, and look at the first word of it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{میں} after a noun}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کمرے} \ur{میں}} — \emph{kamre meṅ} — \textbf{in the room.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{پانی} \ur{میں}} — \emph{pānī meṅ} — \textbf{in the water.}
\end{quote}

Twenty-three chapters, and this is the first time anything in this book has been \textbf{inside} anything else.

Notice the noun. \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} became \textbf{\ur{کمرے}} again, because a postposition is following it. That is the rule from two lessons ago, and it will be the rule every time.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same spelling, two different words}]
This word is spelled \textbf{exactly} like the pronoun \textbf{\ur{میں}} you have used since chapter four, and they are unrelated. They are told apart by \textbf{position}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{where it stands} & \textbf{what it is} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
at the head of a clause & \textbf{I} & \emph{maiṅ} \\
after a noun & \textbf{in} & \emph{meṅ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The pronoun comes from Sanskrit \emph{maya}; the postposition from \emph{madhye}, \textquotedblleft{}in the middle of\textquotedblright{}. They fell together on the page because the Urdu script writes no short vowels — which is exactly the difficulty that makes reading Urdu hard and that this book will keep returning to.

Both in one sentence:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میں} \ur{کمرے} \ur{میں} \ur{ہوں}} — \emph{maiṅ kamre meṅ hūṅ} — \textbf{I am in the room.}
\end{quote}

First word, pronoun. Fourth word, postposition. Same three letters.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kamre meṅ}
  \item \emph{pānī meṅ}, then \emph{āsmān meṅ}
  \item both words at once — \emph{maiṅ kamre meṅ hūṅ}
  \item the oblique doing its work — \emph{kamrā}, then \emph{kamre meṅ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you tell the pronoun from the postposition? (\textbf{By where it stands} — head of the clause, or after a noun.) Why do they look identical? (\textbf{The script writes no short vowels}.) And what shape is the noun in front of it? (\textbf{Oblique}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[par]{\ur{پر} (par) — on}

\label{lesson:UR-C23-par}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{in the room}. Then say the joiner from chapter twenty that turns a sentence against the one before it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{پر}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کام} \ur{پر}} — \emph{kām par} — \textbf{at work.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{آسمان} \ur{پر}} — \emph{āsmān par} — \textbf{in the sky} (literally \emph{on} the sky).
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{میں}} puts a thing inside; \textbf{\ur{پر}} puts it on top of, or at. Between them they cover most of what an A1 learner needs to say about where something is — and Urdu draws the line in a slightly different place from English, which is why the sky is something you are \emph{on}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: and a second \ur{پر}, which is not this one}]
Urdu does this to the reader twice in one chapter. \textbf{\ur{پر}} is also a joiner meaning \textbf{but} — the everyday rival of the \textbf{\ur{لیکن}} you learned in chapter twenty — and again the two are told apart by where they stand:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{where it stands} & \textbf{what it is} \\
\midrule
after a noun & \textbf{on, at} \\
at the head of a clause & \textbf{but} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One is Sanskrit \emph{upari}, the ancestor of English \textbf{over}. The other is Persian. They are not related and they are spelled identically, which is the same trap \textbf{\ur{میں}} set one lesson ago — and the same lesson: in Urdu, \textbf{position is meaning}.

And, like every postposition, it takes the oblique: \textbf{\ur{کمرے} \ur{پر}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kām par}
  \item the pair — \emph{kamre meṅ}, then \emph{kamre par}
  \item \emph{āsmān par}
  \item the other \ur{پر}, at the head — \emph{par …}, and its rival \emph{lekin …}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which postposition puts a thing inside, and which on top? (\textbf{\ur{میں}} and \textbf{\ur{پر}}.) What else does \textbf{\ur{پر}} mean, and how do you tell? (\textbf{But} — by standing at the head of a clause.) And which English word is its Sanskrit cousin? (\textbf{Over}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kamre · ko · meṅ · par]{Into, onto, and to}

\label{lesson:UR-R23-into-and-onto}



\begin{quote}
One rule ran under every lesson in this chapter. State it, then name the three postpositions that made it visible.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the shape-change, bare — \emph{kamrā}, then \emph{kamre}
  \item \emph{Say it:} all three — \emph{kamre ko}, \emph{kamre meṅ}, \emph{kamre par}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the sentence with both spellings of one word — \emph{maiṅ kamre meṅ hūṅ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the joiner that heads a reason — \emph{kyūṅki}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — everything this book owns, put somewhere}
Until this chapter nothing in this book could be anywhere. Every postposition the book has ever shown you — \textbf{\ur{کا}} since chapter three, \textbf{\ur{کے} \ur{لیے}} since chapter twenty-one — was quietly demanding the same shape-change and never said so. Run all of it, cold.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the foods, placed — \emph{pānī meṅ}, \emph{roṭī kamre meṅ}, \emph{ām kamre meṅ}
  \item the weather, placed — \emph{hawā kamre meṅ}, \emph{āsmān par}
  \item with an adjective that follows the noun over — \emph{kāle kamre meṅ}, \emph{purāne kamre meṅ}, \emph{nīle kamre meṅ}
  \item people, marked — \emph{māṅ ko}, and the older fused one, \emph{mujhe}
  \item the postpositions you already had — \emph{āp kā nām}, \emph{kamre ke liye}
  \item pointing and placing at once — \emph{yih kamrā}, then \emph{is kamre meṅ} … which is the next chapter
  \item the two words spelled \ur{میں} — \emph{maiṅ}, then \emph{meṅ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What must a noun do before a postposition? (\textbf{Take the oblique shape}.) Does the adjective follow? (\textbf{Yes}.) Which nouns show no visible change? (\textbf{Those not ending in -\ur{ا}}.) And which two words in this chapter are each spelled like something else entirely? (\textbf{\ur{میں}} and \textbf{\ur{پر}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
